On this one, scrolling IS the ski run.

Powderhorn Basin is a concept build from my portfolio: a fictional cat and heli skiing operation above an invented BC town. The homepage is one mountain descended by scroll. An altimeter ticks down from the 2,610 metre drop-in while the light walks from dawn alpenglow through storm grey to valley lamplight, and by the time you reach the book button, you've already taken the run.

Under the cinema, the practical layer holds: accessibility scores of 100 on all 28 pages, and the packages page answers seats, deposits, and weather days before it asks for anything.

The operation is invented. The system is real, and it's built for any operator whose mountain deserves better than a contact form.

caption:
If a customer cannot buy at the price you advertise, that is a legal problem, not a marketing one.

Since June 2022 it has been a false or misleading representation under the Competition Act to advertise a price nobody can actually pay. In January the Federal Court of Appeal upheld a $38.9 million penalty over a $1.50 booking fee. The fee was disclosed. It was disclosed too late to matter.

The only charges allowed outside your advertised price are ones a statute charges the buyer. There is no small business exemption.

Swipe through, then walk your own checkout on a phone.

Five questions your website should answer before anyone picks up the phone.

What will this cost. What actually happens next. Who this is not for. Whether I can get in the door. And why I should believe any of it.

Every example in here comes off a concept build: ten jobs priced with a sample invoice anyone can read, the three hours of a colour appointment written out, three plain refusals each with its reason, access facts down to the door width. The businesses are invented. The systems are not.

Which one is missing from yours?

The fastest way to be believed is to say plainly what you are not for.

Every business page in every town says the same four things. Passionate. Family owned. Quality work. Years of experience. Worn so smooth they carry no information at all.

On a salon concept I built there is a section headed "who this is not for": no same-day colour, no extensions, no guaranteed match to a photograph, each with its reason. Three refusals, and every one makes the rest of the page more believable.

What is the one job you would rather send down the road?
